item.text: {"question_id":"5B.3","answer":"In 2023, the Sisi administration operated amid severe macroeconomic stress and adopted partial rule-based responses. The government’s IMF-linked program included flexible exchange-rate arrangements, state-asset sales, social-spending commitments, and transparency conditions; it also announced a plan to list state-owned companies. These measures reflected government choices but also IMF conditionality and action by central-bank and other institutions, so attribution to Sisi personally is indirect (BATCH-0022-E013; BATCH-0006-E005; BATCH-0006-E006; BATCH-0001-E005). The 2023 record identifies a state budget law formally associated with the presidency, but supplies no budget amounts, execution evidence, or debt-rule compliance data (BATCH-0013-E001). Outcomes and implementation evidence weigh against concluding that credible rules protected stability: inflation reached 39.7 percent, Egypt was assessed as highly debt-vulnerable, and financing obligations were approximately $28 billion in maturing debt and interest by year-end, with further obligations in 2024 (BATCH-0007-E020; BATCH-0009-R07-E009; BATCH-0009-R11-E008). The IMF reviews were postponed after transparency criteria were not met; military-owned businesses remained opaque, and debt held by state-owned enterprises and their audits were inaccessible or unpublished (BATCH-0009-R07-E009; BATCH-0002-E005). The pound’s roughly 50 percent depreciation and related rate and exchange-rate measures largely began in 2022 and should be treated as pre-2023 context rather than wholly as 2023 action or outcome (BATCH-0001-E005; BATCH-0022-E013). Overall, the evidence supports crisis adjustment and some formal safeguards, but not sustained compliance with credible fiscal, debt, monetary, and financial rules that protected macroeconomic
